task_plan.title: Visual Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem
task_plan.description: A concise, visual-first exploration of the Pythagorean theorem. Instead of heavy algebra, we focus on geometric rearrangements and area-based proofs that make the relationship $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ intuitive and clear.

tasks.task_description: A quick refresher on the components of a right-angled triangle (legs and hypotenuse) and the core statement of the theorem.
Explore the classic 'rearrangement' proof using four identical right triangles within a larger square to visually demonstrate that the area of the hypotenuse square equals the sum of the other two.

chunk: Welcome to the course **Visual Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem**! We are going to explore

one of the most famous relationships in mathematics by using our eyes and intuition, rather than just memorizing formulas.

## Task

1.1: The Right Triangle Foundation

Before we can look at proofs, we need to be experts on the "
star of the show": the **Right Triangle**. Every visual proof we study relies on the specific way this triangle is built

.

A right triangle is defined by having exactly one angle that measures $90^\circ$ (a right angle),
which looks like the corner of a square. This corner is the anchor for the entire theorem. <span class="memory
-ref" data-type="profileMemory">(Tailored for high school geometry basics)

="definition">

In a right triangle, we give specific names to the three sides based on their

relationship to the $90^\circ$ angle:

  • Legs ($a$
and $b$): These are the two sides that meet to form the right angle. They are perpendicular to each other.
• Hypotenuse ($c$): This is the longest side of the triangle, located directly across
from the right angle. It "connects" the two legs.

<diagram data-placeholder-id="dg_b0e2a0abf898" data-subtype="gemini_image" data-layout="right" data-status="pending" data-caption="Anatomy of a Right Triangle"></diagram>

Understanding these labels is crucial because the Pythagorean Theorem describes a relationship between the squares of

these specific lengths. 

<div content-section="key_points">
    <ul>
        <li>The <strong>right

angle is usually marked with a small square symbol.
  • The hypotenuse is always the longest side

.
  • It doesn't matter which leg you call $a$ or $b$, but the
hypotenuse must always be $c$.
<diagram data-placeholder-id="dg_80abe0d531ea" data-subtype="mermaid" data-layout="block" data-status="pending" data-caption="Structural components of the triangle"></diagram>
To move from simple lines to a "visual proof," we have to stop thinking of $a$, $b$, and $c$ just

as lengths and start thinking of them as the sides of squares.

**Are you ready to see how these three sides relate

Welcome to the course **Visual Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem**! We are going to explore one of the most famous relationships in mathematics by using our eyes and intuition, rather than just memorizing formulas. ## Task 1.1: The Right Triangle Foundation Before we can look at proofs, we need to be experts on the "star of the show": the **Right Triangle**. Every visual proof we study relies on the specific way this triangle is built. A right triangle is defined by having exactly one angle that measures $90^\circ$ (a right angle), which looks like the corner of a square. This corner is the anchor for the entire theorem. (Tailored for high school geometry basics)

In a right triangle, we give specific names to the three sides based on their relationship to the $90^\circ$ angle:

  • Legs ($a$ and $b$): These are the two sides that meet to form the right angle. They are perpendicular to each other.
  • Hypotenuse ($c$): This is the longest side of the triangle, located directly across from the right angle. It "connects" the two legs.
Understanding these labels is crucial because the Pythagorean Theorem describes a relationship between the squares of these specific lengths.
  • The right angle is usually marked with a small square symbol.
  • The hypotenuse is always the longest side.
  • It doesn't matter which leg you call $a$ or $b$, but the hypotenuse must always be $c$.
To move from simple lines to a "visual proof," we have to stop thinking of $a$, $b$, and $c$ just as lengths and start thinking of them as the sides of squares. **Are you ready to see how these three sides relate to areas and the famous $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ formula?**

## Task 1.1

: The Area Relationship ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$)

Now that we know the anatomy
of a right triangle, let’s look at the actual "magic" of the Pythagorean Theorem. The formula $a^2

+ b^2 = c^2$ isn't just about numbers; it represents physical **space**.

When
we say "$a$ squared" ($a^2$), we are literally talking about the area of a square where every

side has a length of $a$. Imagine drawing a square attached to each side of our right triangle.

<div content-

section="core_equations">

The Pythagorean Theorem states:

$$

Area_a + Area_b = Area_c$$

Where:

• Area A: The square built on leg $a$.
  • Area B: The

square built on leg $b$.
  • Area C: The square built on the hypotenuse
$c$.

<diagram data-placeholder-id="dg_022084b4e6d6" data-subtype="gemini_image" data-layout="right" data-status="pending" data-caption="Visualizing the Pythagorean Theorem as areas"></diagram>

The total amount of "
paper" needed to cover the two smaller squares (on sides $a$ and $b$) is exactly the same amount

of "paper" needed to cover the big square on the longest side ($c$).

<div content-section="important_take

aways">
  • Geometry is Algebra: The "exponent 2" in the formula literally

refers to the two dimensions of a square.
  • The Hypotenuse Wins: Because $c$ is the
longest side, its square will always have the largest area, equaling the sum of the other two.
We have now established the foundation of the right triangle and the area relationship.
**Would you like to take a short 2-question quiz to wrap up this foundation, or are you ready to jump
straight into the first visual rearrangement proof?**
